source.title: Stochasticity helps to navigate rough landscapes: comparing gradient-descent-based algorithms in the phase retrieval problem
source.authors: Francesca Mignacco; Pierfrancesco Urbani; Lenka Zdeborov'a

record.file_problem: none; full paper text including appendices is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how stochastic gradient methods affect in-distribution generalization in a new setting: synthetic phase retrieval with a single-layer model.
record.gate_note: The paper reports generalization and training-loss outcomes for gradient descent, SGD, persistent-SGD, and Langevin dynamics. It does not test random-label memorization or the specific benchmark conditions in the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures signal recovery and generalization in synthetic real-valued phase retrieval. None of V1–V8 names this comparison. In particular, its batch-fraction sweeps do not test V5's fixed-epoch comparison on image classifiers or language models; simulation time is not a matched epoch budget across batch fractions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for this phase-retrieval setting: stochasticity improves recovery at low sample complexity, and simulations agree with the high-dimensional continuous-time DMFT predictions. Persistent-SGD retains distinct dynamics in the continuous-time limit; vanilla SGD approaches GD as the learning rate vanishes. Relevance to state-of-the-art deep networks remains future work.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic planted phase-retrieval task with Gaussian measurements, a single-layer model, and spherical constraint or ridge regularization; compares full-batch GD, minibatch SGD variants, and Langevin dynamics rather than the claim versions' stated settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies non-monotonically with minibatch fraction, persistence time, and Langevin temperature; initialization and regularization also affect the reported dynamics.

fits_no_version.finding: At t=1000, 9% of GD seeds, 30% of vanilla-SGD seeds and 99% of persistent-SGD seeds reach training loss below 10^-7. Magnetization trajectories also favor the stochastic methods. From random initialization at alpha=2.5, persistent-SGD reaches perfect recovery for the displayed sizes while GD remains on plateaus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stochastic gradient methods can improve signal recovery and generalization over full-batch GD in planted phase retrieval at low sample complexity.

fits_no_version.finding: Persistent-SGD performs best at intermediate batch fractions and persistence times in the tested sweeps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Phase-retrieval generalization depends non-monotonically on persistent-SGD's batch fraction and persistence time.

fits_no_version.finding: Langevin performance is best at intermediate temperatures in experiments that set temperature to zero at t=700.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise temperature affects phase-retrieval recovery non-monotonically under the tested annealing protocol.

record.problems: The study explicitly focuses on a prototypical phase-retrieval setting and says its relevance to highly overparameterized deep networks is left for future work. Generalization is represented through magnetization under a spherical constraint; plotted sweeps do not provide tabulated values or error bars.
record.rows_left_out: None; retained the explicit comparison, parameter-sweep findings, and random-initialization comparison. Figure-only sweep values remain recorded as figure only.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and its comparison with natural-label held-out performance.
Width beyond interpolation and its effect on test error; input-dimension sweeps and temporal double descent do not test this.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and the effects of tuning or optimizer modifications.
Large-batch penalties under fixed epoch budgets in image classification or language modeling, and recipe adaptations that remove them.
Dropout effects, including training-set size, underfitting and data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap rankings and comparison with other measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The cannot_determine states indicate that these rows cannot establish a listed version, not that their phase-retrieval findings are unreadable. Magnetization is a justified generalization measure under the spherical constraint because test MSE decreases monotonically with it.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label test performance.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
No adaptive optimizer comparison or limited-versus-broader tuning comparison.
Batch size is varied, but the study does not test large versus small batches under a fixed epoch budget on image-classification or language benchmarks.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: full-batch gradient descent
rows.operation_detail: Trained on phase-retrieval measurements from a warm initialization; generalization was tracked through magnetization.
rows.measure: Percentage of seeds reaching training loss below 10−7; magnetization used as the accuracy measure.
rows.value: 9% of seeds reached training loss below 10−7
rows.note: Comparator for multi-pass SGD and persistent-SGD; the text says stochastic variants outperform GD in recovering the signal at the shown time scales.
rows.check: The 9% value correctly records seeds reaching the training-loss threshold, not held-out accuracy or magnetization. It measures none of the listed versions.

rows.subject: multi-pass vanilla SGD
rows.operation_detail: Trained with minibatches sampled with replacement; gradients were rescaled by the minibatch fraction.
rows.measure: Percentage of seeds reaching training loss below 10−7; magnetization used as the accuracy measure.
rows.value: 30% of seeds reached training loss below 10−7
rows.note: The authors report average magnetization between GD and persistent-SGD and describe SGD as outperforming GD in recovery.
rows.check: The 30% value correctly records seeds reaching the training-loss threshold, not held-out accuracy or magnetization. It measures none of the listed versions.

rows.subject: persistent-SGD
rows.operation_detail: Trained with persistent minibatch membership and gradients rescaled by the minibatch fraction.
rows.measure: Percentage of seeds reaching training loss below 10−7; magnetization used as the accuracy measure.
rows.value: 99% of seeds reached training loss below 10−7
rows.note: Authors say persistent-SGD reached magnetization one and zero loss while GD remained in poorer-generalization regions at these time scales.
rows.check: The 99% value correctly records seeds reaching the training-loss threshold, not held-out accuracy or magnetization. It measures none of the listed versions.

rows.subject: persistent-SGD
rows.operation_detail: Varied minibatch fraction while tracking median magnetization and median loss over training time.
rows.measure: Median magnetization and median loss over time; authors state generalization performance is non-monotonic in batch size, with the optimum at an intermediate b.
rows.locator: Figure 4, left panel and accompanying Results text
rows.note: For b = 0.1, learning rate was reduced to η = 0.005; for b = 0.01 and 0.05, it was η = 0.0025. The paper contrasts this result with observations in deep neural networks trained on real datasets.
rows.check: The stated non-monotonic batch-fraction effect is supported, but concerns persistent-SGD in phase retrieval without matched epoch budgets. Include the learning-rate changes in the conditions: 0.005 for b=0.1 and 0.0025 for b=0.01 or 0.05.

relation.reason: The paper discusses neural-network generalization and batch-size findings, but its own experiments concern synthetic phase retrieval and leave relevance to deep networks for future work.

tranche.reason: The phase-retrieval results measure none of V1–V8. The batch-fraction sweep does not test V5's fixed-epoch comparison on image classifiers or language models.

source_check.notes: The 9%, 30%, and 99% values measure seeds crossing a training-loss threshold, not held-out accuracy. Random-initialization recovery is reported for the displayed finite system sizes and time scales.
